subject: English
passage:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The sukiya style of Japanese architecture developed from tea ceremony aesthetics and flourished from the late 16th century onward.
• Shōkin-tei, located on the grounds of the Katsura Imperial Villa in Kyoto, is a historic teahouse built in the mid-17th century.
• It was constructed at the edge of a pond and features a low thatched roof over wooden post-and-beam walls with mud plaster.
• Its interior contains tatami-matted rooms arranged around a central tokonoma.
• A tokonoma is a recessed alcove typically used to display scrolls, flower arrangements, or seasonal objects.
prompt: The student wants to provide a detailed overview of the structures at Shōkin-tei. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: Located in Kyoto, Shōkin-tei was designed with a tokonoma, a recessed alcove typically used to display scrolls, flower arrangements, or seasonal objects.
choices.B: Shōkin-tei, whose structures were built in the sukiya style in Kyoto, was constructed in the mid-17th century.
choices.C: Constructed at the edge of a pond, Shōkin-tei's thatched-roof building of wooden posts and mud plaster features tatami-matted rooms arranged around a recessed alcove called a tokonoma.
choices.D: The builders of Shōkin-tei used wood and mud plaster in its construction in Kyoto.

explanation:
Choice C is the best answer. The sentence effectively provides a detailed overview of the structures at Shōkin-tei, noting that the teahouse was constructed at the edge of a pond and describing its thatched-roof building of wooden posts and mud plaster. It also explains the architectural arrangement, specifying that the building features tatami-matted rooms arranged around a recessed alcove called a tokonoma.

Why D is incorrect:

Choice D is incorrect. The sentence mentions only the building materials (wood and mud plaster) and the location of Shōkin-tei. It doesn't provide a detailed overview of the structures, omitting information about the pondside setting, the thatched roof, and the arrangement of tatami rooms around the tokonoma.
